§ 807.81 When a premarket notification submission is required.




(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:




(1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, 



(i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or 





(ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.








(2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.






(3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification:




(i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process.






(ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.










(b) 




(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which:




(i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or






(ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.








(2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.







(c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter.

verdict.summary:
# Draft regulatory answer — lead time for a premarket notification under 21 CFR Part 807, Subpart E (pin date 2026-11-21)

Prepared by: Regulatory Specialist. Status: draft for review by a qualified regulatory affairs professional and by the responsible sponsor/clinician. This is not legal advice, not medical advice, and not for use in patient care.

## 1. Answer

**90 days (calendar days) before the proposed date of introduction, or delivery for introduction, into interstate commerce for commercial distribution.**

Authority: 21 CFR 807.81(a), Part 807, Subpart E (Premarket Notification Procedures), as in force on 2026-11-21. The operative words are "at least 90 days before." Because the regulation says "at least," 90 days is a floor and not a target: a premarket notification submission received by FDA 89 calendar days before the planned first commercial shipment does not satisfy § 807.81(a). Nothing in Subpart E prohibits submitting earlier than 90 days; earlier is lawful and is the usual practice where the submission date is driven by data lock rather than by the launch date.

The same 90-day premarketing interval appears in the statute the regulation implements, section 510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 360(k)). The statutory text was not retrieved verbatim in this iteration and is cited here as the enabling provision, not as an independently quoted source.

## 2. Governing text, quoted verbatim from the pinned source

21 CFR 807.81 "When a premarket notification submission is required":

> "(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this section, each person who is required to register his establishment pursuant to § 807.20 must submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration at least 90 days before he proposes to begin the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution of a device intended for human use which meets any of the following criteria:
>
> (1) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time; that is, the device is not of the same type as, or is not substantially equivalent to, (i) a device in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or (ii) a device introduced for commercial distribution after May 28, 1976, that has subsequently been reclassified into class I or II.
>
> (2) The device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time by a person required to register, whether or not the device meets the criteria in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.
>
> (3) The device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use. The following constitute significant changes or modifications that require a premarket notification: (i) A change or modification in the device that could significantly affect the safety or effectiveness of the device, e.g., a significant change or modification in design, material, chemical composition, energy source, or manufacturing process. (ii) A major change or modification in the intended use of the device.
>
> (b)(1) A premarket notification under this subpart is not required for a device for which: (i) A premarket approval application under section 515 of the act, or for which a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2) of the act, is pending before the Food and Drug Administration, or (ii) There is a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) cleared under section 515C of the act, provided that the change is consistent with the PCCP.
>
> (2) The appropriate FDA Center Director may determine that the submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 of this chapter satisfies the requirement in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.
>
> (c) In addition to complying with the requirements of this part, owners or operators of device establishments that manufacture radiation-emitting electronic products, as defined in § 1000.3 of this chapter, shall comply with the reporting requirements of part 1002 of this chapter."

Source line as published with the section: "[42 FR 42526, Aug. 23, 1977, as amended at 72 FR 73601, Dec. 28, 2007; 89 FR 18792, Mar. 15, 2024]"

The 90-day figure is stated once, in § 807.81(a), and applies to all three criteria in (a)(1), (a)(2) and (a)(3). There is no separate or shorter lead time for changes under (a)(3); the 90-day interval is the same.

No amendment with an effective date between 2024-03-15 and 2026-11-21 was identified in any source consulted, so the text in force on 2026-11-21 is the text quoted in §2.

Residual risk to record: the retrieval was made on 2026-11-23, two days after the pin date, so the snapshot is the current text rather than a point-in-time rendering of 2026-11-21. The two-day gap can only matter if a Federal Register document amending § 807.81 was published and made effective inside that window; nothing in the amendment lines of the three versions suggests one. The closing check is a point-in-time query of the eCFR versioner API for title 21, part 807, subpart E at 2026-11-21, confirming that the amendment line still ends at 89 FR 18792.

## 4. What the 90 days runs between

Start point (submission side): the date FDA receives the submission. The regulation says "submit a premarket notification submission to the Food and Drug Administration" and Part 807 contains no mailbox rule, so the interval is measured to FDA's date of receipt, not to a postmark, courier pickup, or the date the sponsor transmits an electronic copy to a third party. Operational rule: take the date on FDA's acknowledgment of receipt as the start of the interval; do not count from the postmark. This is the conservative reading and the only one that cannot fail if FDA's receipt date is later than the sponsor's dispatch date.

End point (marketing side): the proposed date the device is first introduced, or delivered for introduction, into interstate commerce for commercial distribution — i.e. the first commercial shipment or commercial transfer, not the date manufacturing is completed, not the date of contract signature, and not the date of FDA clearance. "Commercial distribution" is a defined term used throughout Part 807 (§ 807.3 contains the definitions for the part); the exact wording of that definition was not retrieved in this iteration and is a verification item (§8), but it does not affect the 90-day figure.

Counting convention: calendar days, not business days. The regulation contains no weekend, holiday or business-day roll rule, so a planned introduction date that falls on a Saturday or a federal holiday does not move the deadline.

## 5. Worked date arithmetic

Rule: latest acceptable FDA receipt date = planned introduction date − 90 calendar days. Each row below was verified in both directions (subtract 90; then add 90 back to the computed date and confirm it returns the planned date).

| Planned introduction / delivery for introduction into interstate commerce | Latest acceptable FDA receipt date (−90 calendar days) | Back-check (+90 days) |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-21 | 2026-08-23 | 2026-08-23 + 90 = 2026-11-21 ✓ |
| 2027-01-04 | 2026-10-06 | 2026-10-06 + 90 = 2027-01-04 ✓ |
| 2027-03-01 | 2026-12-01 | 2026-12-01 + 90 = 2027-03-01 ✓ |
| 2027-06-30 | 2027-04-01 | 2027-04-01 + 90 = 2027-06-30 ✓ |
| 2027-09-15 | 2027-06-17 | 2027-06-17 + 90 = 2027-09-15 ✓ |

Worked example in full: a device whose first commercial shipment is planned for 2026-11-21 must be received by FDA no later than 2026-08-23. Counting forward from 2026-08-23: 8 days remain in August (to 08-31), plus 30 days in September (38), plus 31 days in October (69), plus 21 days in November (90) = 2026-11-21. A submission received 2026-08-24 would be 89 days before the planned shipment and would not satisfy § 807.81(a).

## 6. Related deadlines that are not this deadline — do not substitute one for another

- **FDA's review time.** The 90-day premarketing interval in § 807.81(a) is a submitter obligation measured backwards from the planned shipment date. It is not a promise that FDA will clear the device within 90 days, and clearance is not automatic on day 90. FDA's review-time commitments under the Medical Device User Fee Amendments (MDUFA V commitment letter, FY2023–FY2027) are expressed in FDA days and are performance goals for the Agency, not marketing authorizations; the exact goal figure for traditional 510(k)s was not verified in this iteration. The two quantities both involve the number 90 and must not be conflated: one is calendar days before shipment, the other is a review-clock goal in FDA days.
- **Marketing before clearance.** If FDA has not cleared the submission by the planned shipment date, the shipment cannot lawfully proceed on the strength of having filed 90 days earlier; introducing a device requiring premarket notification without an effective clearance is prohibited (21 U.S.C. 360(k); misbranding under 21 U.S.C. 352(o)). The 90-day rule is a filing deadline, not a marketing authorization.
- **Establishment registration.** Registration under § 807.20 is a separate obligation with its own timing provisions in Part 807 (annual registration window and initial registration; § 807.22). Those provisions were not retrieved verbatim in this iteration and are not the basis of this answer; the 90-day figure below is unaffected by them. Note that § 807.81(a) applies to a person who "is required to register ... pursuant to § 807.20," so registration status is a predicate for the obligation, not a substitute for it.
- **Submission content.** § 807.87 (information required in a premarket notification submission) and § 807.92/§ 807.93 (510(k) summary / 510(k) statement) govern what must be in the submission; § 807.100 governs FDA's substantial-equivalence determination. None of these alters the 90-day lead time.

## 7. When Subpart E does not require this submission at all

Stated so that the 90-day rule is not applied to a device outside its scope:

- **§ 807.81(b)(1)(i):** a PMA under section 515, or a petition to reclassify under section 513(f)(2), is pending before FDA.
- **§ 807.81(b)(1)(ii):** there is a PCCP cleared under section 515C and the change is consistent with that PCCP.
- **§ 807.81(b)(2):** for a change under (a)(3), the appropriate FDA Center Director determines that submission and grant of a written request for an exception or alternative under § 801.128 or § 809.11 satisfies the (a)(3) requirement.
- **§ 807.85(a):** custom devices within section 520(b) of the Act.
- **§ 807.85(b):** distributors placing a device into commercial distribution for the first time under their own name, and repackagers who place their own name on a device without changing other labeling or otherwise affecting the device, where the device was in commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or a premarket notification was filed by another person.
- Additional exemptions from 510(k) exist in the device classification regulations (21 CFR parts 862–892). This answer addresses timing only; it does not determine whether a 510(k) is required for any particular device.
- **§ 807.81(c):** for radiation-emitting electronic products as defined in § 1000.3, the part 1002 reporting requirements apply in addition to Part 807.

## 8. Verification items a reviewer should close before the file is relied on

1. Point-in-time confirm the eCFR text at 2026-11-21 (see §3) and record the returned amendment line in the regulatory file.
2. Confirm the § 807.3 definition of "commercial distribution" verbatim, and confirm whether Part 807 anywhere defines "submitted"/"receipt"; if it does not, record the receipt-date convention in §4 as the sponsor's operating interpretation.
3. Confirm the exact statutory wording of 21 U.S.C. 360(k), including its 90-day language, from the current U.S. Code.
4. Confirm the current MDUFA commitment-letter review goal for traditional 510(k)s if the review timeline is to be quoted anywhere in the same file, and keep it labelled in FDA days.
5. Confirm whether any device-specific provision (a classification regulation in 21 CFR parts 862–892, a guidance document, or a transition provision applicable to this device type) imposes a different or additional premarketing timing obligation.

## 9. Record to place in the regulatory file

For the device in question, record: (a) the planned first-shipment date; (b) that date minus 90 calendar days as the latest acceptable FDA receipt date; (c) an internal buffer ahead of that date for dispatch and for any Refuse-to-Accept cycle, since a refused submission does not stop the clock; (d) the citation "21 CFR 807.81(a), as in force on 2026-11-21, amendment line ending 89 FR 18792 (Mar. 15, 2024)"; and (e) the version-control entries in §3. The single figure to carry forward is **90 calendar days before the proposed introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce**.

verdict.summary:
STATUS OF THIS DOCUMENT
Draft regulatory analysis for review by a qualified clinician and/or regulatory affairs professional. Not medical advice, not for patient care, and not itself a regulatory submission. All figures are calendar days.

=====================================================================
1. THE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 1 — Outer limit for notifying regulatory agencies.
7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case qualifies. With day 0 = the day of first knowledge, the outer limit is the end of day 7.
Governing text (ICH E2A, §III.A.1, quoted verbatim in both source reproductions below): "Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days."

ASK 2 — The constraint that applies if the full period is used.
The follow-up clock does not run from day 0. It runs from the date on which the initial notification is actually made. The interval is 8 additional calendar days, not 7. Health Canada's Food and Drug Regulations C.05.014(2), quoted verbatim in the GUI-0100 page, fixes the anchor unambiguously: "The sponsor shall, within eight days after having informed the Minister under paragraph (1)(b), submit to the Minister a complete report in respect of that information that includes an assessment of the importance and implication of any findings made." Health Canada's guidance restates the same rule: "In cases where the event is fatal or life threatening, the sponsor must submit a complete report to Health Canada within 8 calendar days after the first notification (initial report) to Health Canada of the event."
Consequence: if the initial report goes out on the last permitted day (day 7), the follow-up is due 8 calendar days later. If the initial report goes out earlier, the follow-up moves earlier by the same number of days (e.g., initial on day 2 → follow-up due day 10).

ASK 3 — Day, measured from day 0, by which the follow-up must be provided when the full initial period is used.
DAY 15. Arithmetic: day 0 + 7 calendar days (initial notification outer limit) = day 7; day 7 + 8 additional calendar days = day 15.

CORRECTION TO A WORKING ASSUMPTION IN THE REQUEST ANALYSIS.
The request analysis proposed "a further seven days, i.e., by day 14". That is wrong on the interval: ICH E2A §III.A.1 says "within 8 additional calendar days", and Canada's C.05.014(2) says "within eight days after having informed the Minister". Both give day 15, not day 14. Day 14 would be correct only if the follow-up interval were 7 days. Do not use day 14.

=====================================================================
2. SOURCES, CITED IN FULL WITH VERSION
=====================================================================

S1. ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline E2A: Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting. Recommended for adoption at Step 4 of the ICH process on 27 October 1994; the 1995 "Guidance for Industry ICH Topic E2A" printing. Sections relied on: §III.A.1 (Fatal or Life-Threatening Unexpected ADRs), §III.A.2 (All Other Serious, Unexpected ADRs), §III.A.3 (Minimum Criteria for Reporting).

S2. US Food and Drug Administration. Guidance for Industry: ICH E2A Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting (1995). https://www.hhs.gov/guidance/sites/default/files/hhs-guidance-documents/FDA/E2A-Clinical-Safety-Data-Management--Definitions-and-Standards-for-Expedited-Reporting.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T21:36:34Z, sha256 2242c6e208d5, 17 pages / 28,440 characters, read in full.

S3. Health Canada. Guidance for Industry: ICH Topic E2A — Clinical Safety Data Management: Definitions and Standards for Expedited Reporting (1995). https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/hc-sc/migration/hc-sc/dhp-mps/alt_formats/hpfb-dgpsa/pdf/prodpharma/e2a-eng.pdf — fetched 2026-11-23T21:36:33Z, sha256 8a40c5acf80b, 16 pages / 31,389 characters, read in full.

S4. Health Canada. Guidance document GUI-0100, section "Serious unexpected adverse drug reaction reporting", quoting Food and Drug Regulations (C.R.C., c. 870) C.05.014 and C.01.017. https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/drugs-health-products/compliance-enforcement/good-clinical-practices/guidance-documents/guidance-drugs-clinical-trials-human-subjects-gui-0100/serious-unexpected-adverse-drug-reaction-reporting.html — fetched 2026-11-23T21:36:31Z, sha256 3ebca4091865, 11,005 characters, read in full.

S5 (retrieval set only, no passage extracted in this pull, no figure asserted from it here): Commission Guideline 2011/C 172/01 (EU) on the collection, verification and presentation of adverse event/reaction reports; and the EMA post-authorisation document pc_final_06-2010. These are listed so the reviewer knows they were in scope; any EU/EEA-facing use requires the current text to be checked separately.

=====================================================================
3. THE RULE AS STATED, IN THE SOURCES' OWN WORDS
=====================================================================

S2 and S3, §III.A.1 (identical wording): "Regulatory agencies should be notified (e.g., by telephone, facsimile transmission, or in writing) as soon as possible but no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that a case qualifies, followed by as complete a report as possible within 8 additional calendar days."

S2: "This report should include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products."
S3 (same sentence, mandatory phrasing): "This report must include an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products."

S2/S3, §III.A.2, for contrast: "Serious, unexpected reactions (ADRs) that are not fatal or life-threatening must be filed as soon as possible but no later than 15 calendar days after first knowledge by the sponsor that the case meets the minimum criteria for expedited reporting."

S4, C.05.014(1)(b): "if it is fatal or life threatening, within seven days after becoming aware of the information."
S4, C.05.014(2): "The sponsor shall, within eight days after having informed the Minister under paragraph (1)(b), submit to the Minister a complete report in respect of that information that includes an assessment of the importance and implication of any findings made."
S4, guidance restatement: "In cases where the event is fatal or life threatening, the sponsor must submit a complete report to Health Canada within 8 calendar days after the first notification (initial report) to Health Canada of the event. Follow-up reports of fatal or life-threatening reactions must include an assessment of the importance of the event and the implication of any findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar drugs."

S2/S3, §III.A.3 (minimum criteria, verbatim as extracted): "...initial reports should be submitted within the prescribed time as long as the following minimum criteria are met: an identifiable patient; a suspect medicinal product; an identifiable reporting source; and an event or outcome that can be identified as serious and unexpected, and for which, in clinical investigation cases, there is..." The extracted passage truncates at this point; the fourth limb in the full guideline text is the requirement, in clinical-investigation cases, of a reasonable suspected causal relationship to the medicinal product. The reviewer should confirm that limb against the full text of §III.A.3 before this analysis is relied on for a specific case.

=====================================================================
4. DAY-COUNTING CONVENTION AND ARITHMETIC
=====================================================================

Day 0 = the date on which the sponsor first has knowledge that the case meets the §III.A.3 minimum criteria for expedited reporting. It is not the date of the event, not the date the full case file is complete, and not the date the case is entered in the safety database.

Convention adopted: day 0 is counted as day zero; the "7 calendar days after first knowledge" interval closes at the end of day 7. The guideline states the interval ("7 calendar days after first knowledge") but does not itself prescribe a labelling convention; under the alternative convention in which the day after first knowledge is called day 1, the same calendar date results and only the label changes. The calendar date, not the label, is what the agency records.

Worked example (calendar days):
  Day 0  = Monday 3 March 2025 — sponsor first has knowledge that the case qualifies.
  Day 7  = Monday 10 March 2025 — outer limit for the initial notification (ask 1).
  Day 15 = Tuesday 18 March 2025 — outer limit for the as-complete-as-possible follow-up, because 10 March + 8 calendar days = 18 March (ask 3).

Sensitivity of the follow-up date to when the initial report is actually sent (all intervals 8 calendar days from the initial notification):
  Initial sent day 0 → follow-up due day 8.
  Initial sent day 2 → follow-up due day 10.
  Initial sent day 7 (the case in the question, "full period used") → follow-up due day 15.

=====================================================================
5. WHY "DAY 8" IS NOT THE ANSWER, AND WHAT THE ABSENCE PROOF SHOWS
=====================================================================

The harness searched the full text of S2, S3 and S4 and found none of "day 8", "8th day", "eighth day", "day eight" (S2: 17 pages / 28,440 characters, sha256 2242c6e208d5; S3: 16 pages / 31,389 characters, sha256 8a40c5acf80b; S4: 11,005 characters, sha256 3ebca4091865).

That absence is consistent with, and supports, the answer of day 15. In the sources the numeral 8 is a duration appended to the date of the initial notification ("8 additional calendar days"; "within eight days after having informed the Minister"), never a day number counted from day 0. A deadline of "day 8" would arise only in the one scenario the question excludes — an initial report sent on day 0. The pages do state both intervals from which the day-15 deadline is derived, so the answer to ask 3 is not that the sources are silent; ask 3 is therefore answered, not listed as not stated.

=====================================================================
6. POPULATION, DOSE AND EXPOSURE
=====================================================================

Population: any subject or patient in a clinical investigation, or any patient in a spontaneous or literature report, of any age (including paediatric) and either sex, any indication, any route. The reporting clock is triggered by the case's qualification under §III.A.1/§III.A.3 (serious, unexpected, and — for clinical-investigation cases — a reasonable suspected causal relationship), not by the patient's characteristics.
Dose or exposure: none enters the calculation. ICH E2A's serious-adverse-event definition is expressly dose-independent ("any untoward medical occurrence that at any dose"), and no dose, concentration, AUC or exposure figure appears in the 7-day or 8-day rule. Accordingly no dose or exposure value is stated in this analysis, and none should be read into the deadlines.
Units: every figure in this document is in calendar days, and every day figure is a day number counted from day 0 unless it is explicitly labelled as an interval added to the initial notification date.

=====================================================================
7. SCOPE OF "REGULATORY AGENCIES"
=====================================================================

ICH E2A §III.A.1 is written for "regulatory agencies" plural and for the "appropriate regulatory authorities": the 7-calendar-day clock runs from a single day 0 for each authority to which the case must be reported, so the day-7 outer limit is not extended by having to notify more than one agency, and the day-15 follow-up limit applies to each of those notifications. The regional rules that fix which authorities are "appropriate" sit outside ICH E2A and are not established by this pull.
Grounded regional confirmation available here: Canada. C.05.014(1)(b) sets 7 days after becoming aware, and C.05.014(2) sets the complete report within 8 days after informing the Minister — the same day-7 / day-15 pair.
Not established here: US, EU/EEA and other national implementing texts. No figure is asserted from them in this document. Before any submission in those jurisdictions, the reviewer must check the current national text (in the US, the IND safety-reporting provisions of 21 CFR 312.32; in the EU/EEA, the current Clinical Trials Regulation and the Commission Guideline cited as S5), because a national rule may impose a shorter period or a different day-counting convention, and the shorter period would govern.

=====================================================================
8. WHAT MUST BE IN EACH OF THE TWO REPORTS
=====================================================================

Initial notification (by day 7): may be by telephone, facsimile transmission or in writing (S2/S3 §III.A.1). It must be filed even though the case is incomplete, provided the §III.A.3 minimum criteria are met (identifiable patient; suspect medicinal product; identifiable reporting source; an event or outcome identifiable as serious and unexpected, plus, in clinical-investigation cases, the causality limb noted in section 3 above).

Follow-up, "as complete a report as possible" (by day 15 when the full initial period is used): must carry "an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings, including relevant previous experience with the same or similar medicinal products" (S2/S3 §III.A.1; C.05.014(2) in S4 uses the same formulation). S3's §III.A administrative data requirements, quoted in the source, require the report to state whether it is an initial or a follow-up (first, second, etc.) report, and require the sponsor's case identification number to be identical across the initial and follow-up reports on the same case — the mechanism by which the day-15 follow-up is linked to the day-7 initial notification.

=====================================================================
9. ITEMS FOR THE REVIEWING CLINICIAN OR REGULATORY PROFESSIONAL TO VERIFY BEFORE USE
=====================================================================

(a) The day-counting convention in the applicable sponsor SOP and in the receiving authority's guidance (section 4). The calendar dates derived here do not change under the two common labelling conventions, but the SOP wording may.
(b) The truncated fourth limb of §III.A.3 as extracted (section 3), read against the full guideline text.
(c) The national implementing text for every jurisdiction in which the case will be filed (section 7); any shorter national period supersedes the day-7 and day-15 figures given here.
(d) Whether the case in hand is fatal/life-threatening (7-day + 8-day rule, the subject of this analysis) or serious-unexpected but neither fatal nor life-threatening (15 calendar days, no 8-day follow-up rule under §III.A.2).

=====================================================================
10. ONE-LINE RESTATEMENT
=====================================================================
Notify the regulatory agency(ies) no later than 7 calendar days after first knowledge that the case qualifies (day 7 from day 0); if that full period is used, provide the as-complete-as-possible follow-up, with an assessment of the importance and implication of the findings and relevant previous experience with the same or similar products, no later than 8 additional calendar days after the initial notification, i.e., by day 15 measured from day 0.

asks.quote: What three-digit serial number must the next submission carry?

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The next submission must carry serial number 018.

DERIVATION

1. The initial IND is serial number 000 — one submission.
2. Seventeen later submissions, all correctly numbered, occupy one continuous sequence: 001, 002, 003, … 017.
3. Highest serial number assigned to date = 017.
4. Next submission = highest assigned + 1 = 017 + 1 = 018, written in the three-digit zero-padded field as 018.

Count cross-check: 1 initial + 17 later = 18 submissions to date. Because the initial carries 000, the serial number equals (submission index − 1): the 18th submission to date carries 017, and the 19th submission — the one now being prepared — carries 018. Both routes (highest-assigned + 1, and submission index − 1) give 018.

GOVERNING RULE AND SOURCES

- 21 CFR Part 312, § 312.23 (IND content and format), as published on eCFR — the provision that governs the content, format and assembly of an IND submission.
- Form FDA 1571, 'Investigational New Drug Application (IND)', field 2 'Serial Number' (current OMB-approved version, OMB control number 0910-0014), which operationalises the convention: the initial IND is assigned serial number 000 and each subsequent submission to that IND is assigned the next number in sequence.
- Convention as stated: three digits, zero-padded; the leading zeros are part of the number and must be retained (000, 007, 018 — never 18). One sequence per IND. The sequence does not restart when the submission type changes.
